                  MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF
                 NORTHERN INDIANA PUBLIC SERVICE COMPANY LLC

       Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC”

or the “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Northern Indiana Public Service

Company LLC (“NIPSCO”) hereby submits this Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer

(“Answer”) to comments and protests filed on January 20, 2026 in response to NIPSCO’s

December 29, 2025 complaint filed in this proceeding (“Complaint”). As discussed below, good

cause exists for the Commission to grant the Motion for Leave and accept this Answer.

I.     EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

       This proceeding was initiated by NIPSCO to establish a rate schedule under the

Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”) Open Access Transmission, Energy

and Operating Reserve Markets Tariff (“OATT” or “Tariff”) to provide a mechanism for NIPSCO

to recover all costs associated with NIPSCO’s compliance with a recent order from the U.S.

Secretary of Energy.2 In that order, the U.S. Secretary of Energy determined, pursuant to section




       1
           18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 213 (2026).
       2
           U.S. Department of Energy, Order No. 202-25-12 (issued Dec. 23, 2025) (“DOE 202(c) Order”).
 202(c) of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”)3 and section 301(b) of the Department of Energy

Organization Act,4 that “an emergency exists in portions of the Midwest region of the United States

due to a shortage of electric energy, a shortage of facilities for the generation of electricity, and

other causes” and that “continued additional dispatch” of NIPSCO’s R.M. Schahfer Generating

Station Units 17 and 18 (“Impacted Schahfer Units”) “is necessary to best meet the emergency

arising from increased demand, determined shortage, and other causes, and serve the public

interest under FPA section 202(c).”5 The DOE 202(c) Order directs MISO and NIPSCO to “take

all measures necessary to ensure” that the Impacted Schahfer Units, which had been scheduled to

retire on December 31, 2025, continue to operate.6

        The Commission has previously determined that the MISO OATT does not contain a rate

recovery mechanism for NIPSCO to recover its costs to comply with the DOE 202(c) Order.7

Indeed, MISO has agreed that its OATT does not contain such a mechanism.8 Accordingly,

NIPSCO filed the instant complaint for the limited purpose of including in the MISO Tariff a new

schedule to effectuate the cost recovery mechanism. The comments and protests raise issues that

are outside the scope of this proceeding and impinge on NIPSCO’s constitutional and statutory

rights to recover costs associated with the DOE 202(c) Order.9

        Many of the protests largely rest on challenges to the lawfulness of the DOE 202(c) Order.

Those arguments are outside the scope of this proceeding and amount to an impermissible

collateral attack on action taken by the U.S. Secretary of Energy. As the Commission has made

clear, including in Consumers Energy, proceedings of this type are limited to whether it is just and

reasonable to require a tariff mechanism that permits recovery of costs incurred to comply with a

DOE 202(c) order. Questions regarding the validity of the DOE 202(c) Order itself fall outside

the Commission’s purview in this context and should not be considered here.

       Consistent with Consumers Energy, the Commission’s task is limited to evaluating whether

MISO should be directed to implement a cost recovery mechanism that enables NIPSCO to recover

costs associated with complying with the DOE 202(c) Order. The Commission should therefore

decline to address arguments challenging the scope, justification, or legality of the DOE 202(c)

Order, as well as speculative arguments concerning potential refunds or rehearing outcomes.

Those issues, if they arise at all, belong in other forums and proceedings.

       There is also no basis for delaying Commission action on the Complaint. Granting the

requested relief would not approve or prejudge any specific costs, nor would it foreclose any party

from later challenging the prudence or recoverability of particular expenditures. NIPSCO seeks

only the establishment of a tariff mechanism. NIPSCO has clearly stated that it will submit a

subsequent filing to support recovery of specific costs, net of market revenues, which will provide

interested parties with a full opportunity to review and contest those costs. Establishing a

mechanism now does not prejudice any party’s rights.

Out-of-Time Comments of the Illinois Commerce Commission under EL26-36 (filed Jan. 21, 2026) (“ICC
Comments”).

        Moreover, the DOE 202(c) Order remains fully effective. No subsequent DOE action or

judicial decision has stayed or limited its application. The Order expressly directs NIPSCO to file

revisions with the Commission to effectuate cost recovery and requires NIPSCO and MISO to take

all measures necessary to ensure continued operation of the Schahfer Impacted Units. NIPSCO is

incurring significant capital, operating, and maintenance costs to comply with these directives.

Delaying action would undermine NIPSCO’s ability to recover costs it is legally obligated to incur.

The Commission’s authority to act on the requested tariff revisions now does not depend on any

later determination regarding the validity of the DOE Order in another forum.

       Intervenors’ objections to the proposed cost recovery mechanism itself are likewise

unavailing. MISO has acknowledged that its Tariff does not currently include a mechanism that

would allow cost recovery as contemplated by the DOE 202(c) Order. General references to

existing market compensation for energy, capacity, or ancillary services do not address the unique

circumstances of costs incurred pursuant to a section 202(c) emergency order. Where MISO, as

the administrator and expert on its own Tariff, confirms that no such mechanism exists, the

Commission should defer to that judgment.

       Commission precedent also supports allocating costs in accordance with the geographic

and substantive scope of the emergency identified by DOE.            In Consumers Energy, the

Commission found it just and reasonable to allocate costs based on the scope of the emergency

described in the DOE Order, without requiring a separate demonstration of cost causation or

quantified benefits.10 Here, DOE similarly identified resource adequacy concerns in MISO’s

northern and central regions based on the Planning Resource Auction results. Directing MISO to




       10
            Consumers Energy at P 39.


                                                -4-
 implement a tariff mechanism that allocates costs consistent with that determination is therefore

just and reasonable.

       Requests for additional procedural safeguards, reporting requirements, or clawback

provisions are unnecessary and outside the scope of this proceeding. The proposed mechanism

already limits recovery to costs incurred during the order duration period and requires Commission

approval of specific costs in a later filing, net of market revenues.          Imposing additional

requirements at this stage would improperly prejudge future cost recovery issues and would be

unduly discriminatory given that similar conditions were not imposed in comparable proceedings.

       Finally, the Commission should reject calls to defer action pending a MISO stakeholder

process.    Section 202(c) assigns responsibility for addressing rate recovery issues to the

Commission, not to MISO stakeholder processes. Interested parties had a full opportunity to

comment in this proceeding, and further delay would only postpone necessary relief. MISO itself

supports adding a cost recovery schedule to the Tariff and has not requested a stakeholder process

as a prerequisite to Commission action. Granting the Complaint will not prevent MISO from

pursuing broader stakeholder discussions in the future, so long as those efforts do not delay timely

implementation of the required cost recovery mechanism sought here.

       For all of these reasons, the Commission should reject the arguments raised in the protests

and grant the Complaint.

II.    MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

       NIPSCO respectfully requests that the Commission waive Rule 213 of its Procedural

Rules and accept this Answer.11 Waiver has been granted when the Answer would ensure an




       11
          18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2) (“An answer may not be made to a protest, an answer, a motion for
oral argument, or a request for rehearing, unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority”).


                                                -5-
 accurate and complete record, assist the Commission in its decision-making process, provide

information helpful to the disposition of an issue or permit the issues to be narrowed or

clarified.12 Waiver is appropriate here because this Answer will assist the Commission in its

review of NIPSCO’s Complaint and will provide useful and relevant information that will help

ensure an accurate record in this proceeding.               NIPSCO specifically responds to certain

misstatements and inaccuracies in the protests and clarifies certain aspects of its request to add

a means for cost recovery to the MISO Tariff. NIPSCO therefore submits that good cause exists

for the Commission to accept this Answer.

III.    ANSWER

        A.         Challenges to the DOE 202(c) Order Are Outside the Scope of this
                   Proceeding

        Both the Michigan AG Protest and the PIOs Protest urge the Commission to deny

NIPSCO’s Complaint on the grounds that the DOE 202(c) Order is ultra vires.13 The PIOs devote

an entire section to challenging the lawfulness of the DOE 202(c) Order, arguing that it “addresses

circumstances beyond the lawful scope of an emergency under Section 202(c) and fails to provide

evidence or reasoned decision-making substantiating the existence of an emergency.”14 Similarly,

 the Michigan AG contends that NIPSCO is not entitled to cost recovery if DOE grants rehearing

and the order is found to be invalid, as the “DOE Order [is] an attempt by DOE to illegally and

arbitrarily usurp the decided roles…in resource adequacy planning.”15

      These arguments, however, are outside the scope of this proceeding and amount to a

collateral attack on the lawfulness of action taken by the U.S. Secretary of Energy, which is beyond

the Commission’s purview. As the Commission explained in Consumers Energy:

        Arguments against adoption of the Proposed Tariff Provision, such as that imposing
        the costs of keeping the Campbell Plant in operation violates the Tariff and the FPA
        if the DOE Order is deemed unlawful are beyond the limited scope of this
        proceeding . . .16

      Similar to the complaint in Consumers Energy, NIPSCO requests that the Commission

require MISO to revise its Tariff to include a cost recovery mechanism to allow NIPSCO to recover

its costs associated with complying with DOE’s order. By its own precedent, the Commission’s

analysis here is limited to the reasonableness of the request to direct MISO to implement a cost

recovery mechanism, and any consideration of the lawfulness of DOE’s action or the validity of

the DOE 202(c) Order itself is outside the scope of this proceeding. Accordingly, consistent with

Consumers Energy, the Commission should decline to consider these arguments.

        Michigan AG and PIOs further argue that the Commission should delay ruling on

NIPSCO’s Complaint and the establishment of a cost recovery mechanism.17 They provide no

basis for such a delay, while there are multiple reasons supporting timely Commission action.

exhausted.”).

         First, granting the Complaint would not automatically permit NIPSCO to recover costs

associated with the Schahfer Impacted Units, and no party would be foreclosed from challenging

specific costs in a later proceeding.18 NIPSCO asks that the Commission direct MISO to add a

cost recovery mechanism for 202(c) related costs, not for the Commission to approve any specific

costs.19 As NIPSCO previously explained, it intends to submit a subsequent filing to support the

costs associated with the continued operation of the Schahfer Impacted Units, which will provide

stakeholders with an opportunity to review and evaluate those costs.20 Granting NIPSCO’s

complaint and directing MISO to add a cost recovery mechanism to its Tariff therefore does not

prejudice any party’s ability to challenge the appropriateness of the costs NIPSCO seeks to recover

in future proceedings.

        Second, there have been no subsequent orders from DOE or any judicial authority that

pause or limit the effectiveness of the DOE 202(c) Order. The DOE 202(c) Order directs NIPSCO

to “file with [FERC] revisions or waivers to effectuate this Order,” and states that rate recovery is

available under the FPA.21 It further “directs MISO and NIPSCO to ‘take all measures necessary

to ensure’ that the Impacted Schahfer Units…continue to operate.”22 Consistent with these

directives, NIPSCO has made, and will continue to make for the appropriate period, necessary

capital investments and incur operating and maintenance expenses, and therefore requires a cost

recovery mechanism. There is no basis for delaying implementation of NIPSCO’s requested cost

stakeholders with an opportunity to evaluate such costs).

 recovery mechanism which is intended to protect NIPSCO’s constitutional and statutory right to

recover costs associated with the DOE 202(c) Order.

       If NIPSCO were not to take steps to effectuate the DOE 202(c) Order by seeking a cost

recovery mechanism and continuing to incur costs necessary to make the Schahfer Impacted Units

operational, it could risk noncompliance with the DOE 202(c) Order and be subject to severe

penalties. Under the FPA, “[a]ny person who violates any provision…of any rule or order…shall be

subject to a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day such violation continues.”23

Regardless of protesters’ assertions, the DOE 202(c) Order remains in effect, and as noted, neither

DOE nor any court has stayed or limited its application. The Commission’s ability to implement the

rate schedule and, in the future, allow cost recovery does not hinge on any later determination of the

DOE 202(c) Order’s validity. For these reasons, there is no basis for delaying Commission action.

       Finally, the Michigan AG argues that, pursuant to the filed rate doctrine, any recovery of

FPA 202(c) associated costs would need to be refunded if the DOE 202(c) Order were vacated.24

Likewise, the PIOs ask the Commission to clarify that all costs recovered under the new tariff

provision would be subject to refund.25 As discussed above, NIPSCO seeks only approval of a

mechanism by which such costs may be recovered. NIPSCO will submit a separate filing to seek

recovery of any specific costs incurred under the rate recovery mechanism. As with protesters’

other arguments, questions regarding the lawfulness of the DOE 202(c) Order or potential refunds

are entirely outside the scope of this proceeding and should not be addressed here.

         B.         NIPSCO’s Proposed Cost Recovery Mechanism is Appropriate and
                   Consistent with the DOE 202(c) Order

        Intervenors make several unavailing arguments about NIPSCO’s proposed cost recovery

mechanism. First, certain intervenors argue that the MISO Tariff already provides appropriate

cost recovery for NIPSCO.26 Second, intervenors argue that the Commission must specifically

identify the costs and benefits associated with the continued operation of the Schahfer Impacted

Units consistent with cost causation principles.27 Finally, several intervenors request that the

Commission set the matter for hearing, and/or establish additional procedures and reporting

requirements within NIPSCO’s cost recovery mechanism.28 The Commission should find each of

these arguments to be unpersuasive and should find, as it did in Consumers Energy, that the

proposed cost allocation methodology is appropriate and consistent with the DOE 202(c) Order.29

                   1.      MISO Agrees That Its Tariff Does Not Currently Include a
                           Mechanism to Allow Cost Recovery Pursuant to the DOE 202(c)
                           Order

        PIOs argue that the MISO Tariff will already “adequately compensate” NIPSCO for

providing energy and ancillary services and that no further cost recovery mechanism is necessary

until NIPSCO can demonstrate that the MISO Tariff itself will not adequately provide cost

recovery.30 The Commission should reject this argument. In its Answer, MISO acknowledged

remove the “before and” language for MISO’s submittal of the Schedule 56.

contemplated by the DOE Order.”31 A vague reference to the fact that MISO’s Tariff already

contains rules governing the capacity and ancillary services markets ignores the specific details of

this case and the purpose of this proceeding.

        NIPSCO was directed to operate the Schahfer Impacted Units specifically under the

emergency circumstances outlined by DOE under section 202(c) of the FPA.32 In this proceeding,

NIPSCO is seeking a recovery mechanism in the MISO Tariff to permit NIPSCO to recover costs

associated with complying with the DOE 202(c) Order, as is specifically contemplated by the

language of section 202(c) and the DOE 202(c) Order itself.33 NIPSCO clearly specified that it

intends to submit a subsequent filing with the Commission pursuant to FPA section 202(c), in

which NIPSCO will explain and support its just and reasonable costs associated with operating the

Impacted Schahfer Units and complying with the DOE 202(c) Order, netting out any applicable

market revenues.34 Accordingly, the amount that will be recovered through the MISO markets is

outside the scope of this proceeding and the existing general MISO market rules are not helpful

for this specific inquiry. MISO is the administrator of and expert on its own Tariff. If MISO

determines that there is no mechanism within its own Tariff to allow cost recovery as required by

the DOE 202(c) Order, then the Commission should defer to MISO’s judgment and expertise on

that matter.

        Finally, the Commission should find PIOs’ attempt to distinguish “cost recovery” and “rate

recovery” unpersuasive. The PIOs seek to manufacture a distinction that has no meaningful

application in this context. Under the terms of section 202(c), entities subject to an emergency

order are entitled to “compensation or reimbursement” in the event the terms of an arrangement

cannot be agreed upon, as is the case here. NIPSCO’s proposed recovery mechanism implements

that statutory entitlement through a construct within the MISO Tariff that allows for NIPSCO’s

costs to be allocated across MISO’s North and Central regions, consistent with Commission

precedent and permitted by the text of section 202(c).

                 2.     Commission Precedent Supports Allocating Costs in Accordance with
                        the Scope of the DOE-Prescribed Emergency

       PIOs argue that the Commission should examine whether the relief requested would

impose cost increases on ratepayers without commensurate benefit, and therefore whether the

proposed cost recovery is consistent with cost causation principles. Similarly, OMS requests that

the Commission exercise its authority to establish hearing procedures to review the cost recovery

mechanism.35 However, PIOs and OMS ignore the Commission’s finding in Consumers Energy

that it is “just and reasonable for the cost allocation method to allocate costs in accordance with

the scope of the emergency as described by the DOE Order.”36 The Commission did not require

specific demonstration of costs and benefits nor did it set the matter for hearing in the Consumers

Energy proceeding, and it should not do either of those things here.

       In Consumers Energy, the Commission clearly specified that it is appropriate to allocate

costs on the basis of the DOE 202(c) order and did not require the recipient of the 202(c) order to




       35
            OMS Comments at 4.
       36
            Consumers Energy at P 39.


                                               -12-
 specifically demonstrate cost causation or benefits or set the matter for hearing.37 In Consumers

Energy, the Commission stated that “it is reasonable to interpret the DOE Order’s reliance on

statements in MISO’s presentation on the Planning Resource Auction Results for Planning Year

2025-2026 that ‘new capacity additions were insufficient to offset the negative impacts of

decreased accreditation, suspension/retirements and external resources’” in the MISO North and

Central regions as indicating that resource adequacy concerns for those regions were the driver for

the DOE Order.”38 So too here, in NIPSCO’s DOE 202(c) Order, DOE specifically referenced the

same reported results of the Planning Resource Auction for the 2025-2026 Planning Year to

establish an emergency in MISO’s “northern and central zones.”39 Accordingly, because DOE has

specified the scope of the emergency, it is just and reasonable for the cost allocation methodology

to allocate costs in accordance with the scope of that emergency.

       Calls to set this matter for hearing should be rejected. The Commission has broad

discretion to determine whether an evidentiary hearing is warranted and generally does so only

where there are material facts in dispute. Here, no such dispute exists. Moreover, the Commission

recently issued an order accepting a materially-identical cost recovery mechanism without setting

the matter for hearing. Nothing about this Complaint therefore presents novel or case-specific

factual issues requiring adjudication, and a hearing would serve no purpose.

                  3.       Any Additional Procedural or Reporting Requirements Are
                           Unnecessary

       The Michigan AG requests that the Commission modify the proposed cost recovery

mechanism to ensure any charges pursuant to it are just and reasonable, and add certain

 safeguards.40 However, such additional procedural and reporting requirements are unnecessary,

outside the scope of this proceeding, and given that the Commission did not impose such

requirements on a similarly-situated entity that received a DOE 202(c) order, doing so would be

       Specifically, the Michigan AG argues that the cost recovery mechanism limits cost

recovery to “only those expenditures necessary for its limited scope of operation under the DOE

Order and/or provide a clawback provision to reimburse customers for all or a portion of costs if

the Schahfer Units continue to operate beyond the terms of the DOE Order.”41 However, as

currently drafted, the cost recovery mechanism contains the appropriate safeguards. The cost

recovery mechanism will limit the costs to those incurred during the specific Order Duration

Period42 and specifies that NIPSCO shall petition to FERC to approve the recovery of specific

Order Costs, net of market revenues, that FERC determines are recoverable pursuant to section

202(c). There are therefore already adequate and just and reasonable safeguards within the cost

recovery mechanism that limit recovery to the specific costs incurred to comply with the DOE

202(c) Order. The Michigan AG’s requests for further limitations calls for the Commission to

prejudge which costs are recoverable at this point, which is outside the scope of this proceeding.

Finally, NIPSCO intends for the rate schedule that will be applicable to its recovery for continued

operation of the Schahfer Impacted Units to mirror the rate schedule to be approved for

Consumers Energy. Given the similar nature of these proceedings, requiring any additional

        C.        The Commission Should Not Delay Issuing an Order Granting this Complaint
                  While MISO Determines Whether to Pursue a Stakeholder Process

        The Commission should reject calls requiring a MISO stakeholder process before the

Commission rules on the Complaint. First, a MISO stakeholder process raises the same concerns

of delaying cost recovery as addressing the arguments outside of the scope of this proceeding.

Furthermore, FPA section 202(c) directs the Commission, not MISO, to address the rate recovery

issues arising from the DOE 202(c) Order.43 Interested stakeholders were provided the opportunity

to comment on NIPSCO’s proposed cost recovery schedule in this Complaint proceeding. As

outlined, the majority of those comments focus on collateral attacks beyond the scope of this

proceeding, not specific alternative proposals or revisions. The deadline for comments on the

proposed Tariff schedule has passed.          While NIPSCO does not generally oppose a MISO

stakeholder process and can see the merits in a solution that would be more universally-applicable

rather than piecemeal,44 referral to a MISO stakeholder process prior to a Commission order on

this Complaint would allow intervening parties who chose not to avail themselves of the

opportunity to comment or provide alternatives to delay the important relief NIPSCO is seeking.

        Notably, MISO has not called for a stakeholder process. Instead, MISO expressly states

that it “supports the addition of a cost recovery schedule to the Tariff” and “believes that a

Commission finding that such a mechanism be incorporated in the Tariff” would ensure

 compliance with the DOE 202(c) Order.45 NIPSCO is entitled to cost recovery on a timely basis

       Finally, granting the Complaint will not impede MISO from initiating any broader

stakeholder processes that it may deem appropriate in the future, as long as such processes do not

delay granting the relief NIPSCO has requested in the Complaint.

IV.    CONCLUSION

       For the foregoing reasons, NIPSCO respectfully requests that the Commission consider

this Answer and issue an order granting its Complaint.
